After spending around six months scouring various digital camera reviews online and through magazines, I finally decided on the Canon Powershot A95 5 Megapixel camera as offering the perfect marriage of power and portability. My first digital camera, I bought it as a going-away present for myself, since I was spending the summer living and working in Spain and knew that I needed a camera that could keep up with my travels.

It was a snap to take out and set up, and intuitive enough that a couple of cursory glances at the Quick Start guide had me well on my way to pointing and shooting. The camera comes with a USB cable, several software programs, a 16 MB Compact Flash card (of course, you'll want to invest in more memory as soon as possible - with the highest-resolution photos, consider a 512 MB or larger card), batteries, and a wrist strap.

I would rate the camera as mid-sized. It is not wafer-thin, but neither is it absurdly bulky or heavy. For most of my traveling around Spain, I simply slipped it into its bubble wrap and into a soft fabric bag, where it fit comfortably in my purse. The design is comfortable to shoot with over long periods, and I found the layout of the buttons to be intuitive. Less is more: there are few external buttons (shutter, on/off, menu and related buttons), and most controls are carried out through the on-screen menus. The flip-out LCD screen is one reason I decided on this Canon over others in the PowerShot line; it makes previewing photos a snap, and can be swiveled 180 degrees.

The photo quality (I kept it on large superfine) is astonishing: clear, sharp, vibrant photos (check out some of my uploaded photos using the Canon A95) in true-to-life tones with minute detailing. There are various shooting modes, including manual, macro, panoramic (with Stitch Assist software), nighttime, slow shutter, and more, and a movie mode that captures brief (jerky) videos with tinny sound. This isn't a camcorder, so I wasn't surprised that video quality wasn't better, since I bought this primarily for photos.

You will also want to invest in a few basic accessories: rechargeable NiCad batteries and a rapid charger, a sturdy case, and a bigger memory card, for starters. Although the included software is capable enough to get the job done, consider upgrading to Adobe Photoshop Elements (around $90), or if you're a pro, Adobe PhotoShop CS 2 (several hundred dollars). An excellent first camera with plenty of power and a reliable name.

This AMAZONBASICS FM DUAL ALARM DIGITAL CLOCK RADIO (with USB Charging Port, LED Display) plays FM radio stations only. (It’s not a good choice for a news junkie like myself, as my favorite local news-only stations are all on AM channels.)

The FM radio speaker sounds very tinny, so you won’t want to use the radio to listen to music. It’s okay, I think, for playing FM music to wake you up. If you don’t like the speaker, you can just use the plain alarm-sound option. You can also connect the clock to an auxiliary MP3 device.

The beeper alarm doesn’t sound overly loud to me, even at the maximum volume. It takes many seconds for the volume to increase from the initial faint beep to the maximum. To wake out of a really sound sleep, you need a high-volume alarm.

It’s nice being able to set two different alarms. The alarms are NOT tied to specific days of the week--you just turn on the one you want. One alarm is at the left of the clock, the other is at the right. Two people who rise at different times will like this feature, or one person can use it for something like weekdays and weekends.

The digital display is large enough to read from across a room. However, the display is NOT so bright that it will interfere with sleeping. The time is easy to program by sliding the “Lock” button, holding down the volume button until the correct time is displayed, and sliding the Lock button back to locked position.

Another nice feature is the battery backup. It takes two AAA batteries, and ensures that your alarm will go off on time even if you have a power outage while you’re sleeping.

This IHOME iAV5B COLOR CHANGING BLUETOOTH RECHARGEABLE STEREO SPEAKER SYSTEM FOR AMAZON ECHO DOT adds a colorful light show to my powder room! It’s no space hog—the footprint is only slightly wider than the Echo Dot itself (2nd Generation Dot, see buyer warning note below). The speaker also raises the Dot well above the countertop, so that the Dot’s “active” light ring is much easier to see.

As for the sound, it’s better than the sound from my original Echo (the tall one with built-in speakers). It’s a huge improvement over the tinny Dot speakers. I use the speaker system to play music (from Prime Music, and from my playlist) and environmental sounds (rain, etc.). I also use it as an intercom (“Alexa, Drop in ….”) and for all the usual Alexa tasks (shopping lists, lookup answers, etc.).

The speaker system is very easy to set up. You place your Gen2 Dot into the well, connect it to the internal USB cable, and plug the speaker into a wall outlet using a USB cable and AC adapter. (The cable and adapter are NOT included, but you should already have these—you can use the same ones that came with your Dot.) You then open the Alexa app and use Bluetooth to pair the Dot and the speaker. (If your Dot is already connected to your wireless network, you don’t have to fool with wireless connections at all.)

Once the speaker is plugged in and paired, the buttons on the Dot will turn the power and the mic on and off, and will control the volume. Voice commands will also control the volume. A button on the back of the speaker controls the lightshow (color cycling speed, color changing, on/off). As long as the speaker is charged, you can move it (and the Dot) around your house, and it will operate without being plugged in.

BUYER WARNING NOTE: This speaker system is designed for the 2nd Generation Echo Dot, which has volume buttons on top. The Gen2 Dot drops into a well atop the speaker, and sits flush with the top edge of the speaker. My 1st Generation Dot, which has no volume buttons (you adjust the volume by turning the entire top), does NOT work with this speaker. I was able to force the Gen1 Dot into the well, and to connect it to the speaker’s internal USB cable, but it wouldn’t turn on. (Fortunately I also owned a Gen2 Dot that I could use.)

The speaker system doesn’t seem to be particularly fragile. I connected my Gen1 (unsuccessfully) and Gen2 Dots to the internal cable repeatedly (at least four times) without breaking anything. If you need to disconnect the internal cable, it’s easiest to do it gently with pliers, instead of by prying it loose with a screwdriver (per the instructions).

I had high hopes for this little turntable. It looked perfect for my oldest son who is a huge 80's music fan and thought he should hear it in its original format. We were excited to unbox it and play the two albums we picked up at the used book store. First impressions were OK. The case looks nice and love the two speakers built in. Opening it, we were underwhelmed by the plastic turntable, stylus arm and rather cheap looking controls. But we were still excited.

The sound was also a little disappointing. The two speakers are underpowered and all high end so it was pretty tinny. But the absolute worst was that they stylus is so head light that it skipped constantly. We put a small glass bead on it and the weight actually slowed the turntable. We backed off and placed a quarter on it and it played about right. But again, I was underwhelmed by the underpowered turntable. Also, we noted that one of the spongy pads on the turn table was not installed properly and put a list to the album. We fixed that and fixed the quarter to the stylus and we were able to get it to play through Adam Ant's Friend or Foe album. The scratchy quality of between songs brought me back 40 years to my own first phonograph, which I think was pretty crappy, but probably better than this one.

It works, its nostalgic. We have had fun and will probably get an album at every used bookstore, garage sale, or antique store we find them in, but we will need to upgrade if he goes beyond just enjoying the novelty of it.

Most of the headphones with which I have worked have been active noise canceling (ANC) phones so I know a lot about those, but I also have other headphones too that I like. I was unaware that 3M even had headphones, and I was also unsure what their "Quiet Space" was all about. It's an interesting solution that works fairly well. Overall, these are good phones, though there's one area that could use some slight improvement and that's the sound profile.

These are over-the-ear phones and they are actually quite comfortable. I like how they feel on my head - they fit snugly and I can tilt my head without losing these phones, but they don't clamp down super tight either.

Build-wise, these are more substantial than the price suggests. I like the size adjustment in particular which is designed to last and should not fatigue with use.

I powered these on and they quickly paired and connected to my laptop. The range is good and I was able to walk a fair distance away without losing the connection or having the sound get crackly or having it skip. With no feed coming to them they eventually powered themselves off, saving battery but potentially frustrating the wearer if this is unexpected.

Just putting these on I was surprised by the amount of noise isolation. Without even turning these on they drastically reduced the ambient noise in the room, even effectively blocking out the sound of a running fan. I have had very few headphones that have as effective sound isolation as these, and that's a huge plus right out of the gate. The Quiet Space function adds to this, but not like ANC phones - it injects white noise into the cans so all you hear is a gentle but constant hiss that overrides most other noises. It's not deathly quiet with these on, but you won't hear most other sounds in the area when they're producing white noise. This is a very different approach to sound cancellation and it works.

The sound profile is the one area where these phones could use a little improvement, though these are not terrible and are better than some big-name phones I have used. The bass is not overdriven but it is not muted either, and this is refreshing since most manufacturers overdrive the bass. The highs are clear, though not shrill. The midrange, however, is flat to the point that music can sound slightly hollow. It's an easy fix with an equalizer and is better than one particular big-name manufacturer's similar flaw.

I like these phones and will be working with them more. They take a different approach to dealing with ambient noise and surrounding distractions than what ANC phones use, and they seem to work well. They're well made, comfortable and reasonably priced.

I usually do not use ear buds and favor over-ear headphones when I am listening to music or am traveling. I decided to take a chance on these ear buds based on the fact that they have active noise canceling. These are better than I expected.

These bear a striking resemblance to Apple’s Air Pods which is no accident. Apple makes a great product and at a glance these are very similar.

I popped these in and they immediately were available for pairing. Pairing took almost no time at all and they were ready to go. Some headphones and ear buds take a good bit of time to connect or are hard to discover; these were simple and straightforward. I can’t really ask much more than that.

The ANC function is not on by default, and it turns on and off with a touch and hold on either bud. When it kicks on, the impact is dramatic and immediate. I have a fan that I use for testing ANC headphones, and with it on it faded out nearly completely when I activated ANC on these buds. It is not as aggressive as something like Sony or Bose ANC, but it is good enough to say it’s better than average. With the ANC engaged, listening at low volume levels is easy and background sounds are usually not an issue.

The sound profile is fairly balanced, which is a neat trick for ear buds (particularly with ANC). The highs are very clear and bright, almost to the point of being piercing though not to the pain threshold. The midrange is surprisingly warm and full and music sounds balanced as a result. Bass is present and reasonable which is a rare find anymore since most manufacturers boost bass to uncomfortable levels and usually at the expense of the midrange.

These are surprisingly comfortable for in-ear-canal buds. Usually I struggle with ear buds that fit inside the opening of the ear canal and they either start to hurt after a while or they make my ears itch. These are light and they almost don’t feel like they’re in my ears at all. I actually will wear these more then other buds I have used simply because of how comfortable they are in comparison.

I like that these do not need an app to be adjusted.

These are a pleasant surprise in ear buds for me. They work well, have good sound and the ANC is surprisingly effective. These are priced very competitively too which is a big plus.

I have worked with a lot of ANC headphones, and I have a different pair of JVC phones that have served me well. I looked to these phones as a possible replacement for a dead pair of Bose QC-15 phones that finally just wore out. These are good phones that balance sound quality and ANC nicely.

The ANC function is what interested me most about these and I set about testing them. These work very well but they are not as aggressive as Bose or Sony when it comes to actively cancelling out low-frequency noise. This is a good thing in most cases as the aggressive ANC on Bose and Sony is actually uncomfortable when turned on. Where the two bigger players go all-out for maximum ANC function, these go for "good enough for most" and in terms of how they compare against other manufacturers such as Sennheiser, Philips, and other well-known brands they compare well. They cancel out the lion's share of low droning noises such as road noise and fans, enough so that turning on music at low volumes is still workable in noisy environments.

The sound profile is another important consideration and I have seen a wide variance in sound quality, particularly among ANC phones. These get the sound profile fairly close to right which is a refreshing change. The bass is present and strong but isn't pushed forward as with so many other headphones. The midrange is warm and gives music a decent depth. The highs are clear and bright without being shrill. These aren't audiophile quality phones by any means, but they are better than many I have used.

These are over-the-ear phones which is my preference. I also like that these fit snugly and don't slip off whern I look down which is also a personal preference but it's important to me. If you like a very light set of phones these probably are not quite the right fit for you; if you like a set that fits a bit more firmly, these are good in that regard.

These are comfortable too. The ear cups are padded nicely and I can wear them for a couple of hours before I need to take them off for a few minutes. Most headphones I have worn get uncomfortable after a while, and these do also but it is not as quick as with many.

My one complaint is the way these are powered on and off. Instead of a simple on/off button or switch, the cans swivel to power them on and off. I can see the potential for taking them off and leaving them powered on, resulting in reduced useful runtime.

I like these phones and have been working with them quite a bit of late. They're not a complete replacement for more aggressive ANC phones but they get the sound profile right and they are comfortable enough to wear for a long flight. These strike a nice balance between comfort, ANC capability and sound quality.

I have worked with a lot of active noise canceling (ANC) headphones by a lot of manufacturers, including an older pair of Philips headphones. I’ve seen a wide variance in ANC implementation and sound profiles, and to be honest few manufacturers get theirs right. With this set of headphones, Philips comes close.

These are over-ear phones which I prefer over on-ear phones. They fit snugly but not tight, and they actually do a good job of sound isolation. Even if you don’t like the ANC function (which would defeat the purpose of having these phones), these do a surprisingly good job of sound isolation. The pads are soft enough and comfortable enough that I can wear these for quite a while without discomfort. After a bit of time they do start to get a little warm but not to the point that I need to take them off.

These connect via Bluetooth and they connect very quickly. The connectivity of these phones is absolutely amazing: this is the very first pair of Bluetooth headphones I have used that maintains a steady connection up two flights of stairs with closed doors in between the phones and the source. The connectivity alone makes these very much worth checking out.

The ANC function is very good though it is not quite as aggressive as that of Bose or Sony. It is strong enough to mostly drown out a droning high-volume fan (my baseline for testing), such that music at a low volume while the ANC is turned on completely drowns out the fan. While Bose and Sony go to the extreme for noise cancellation, and other manufacturers often have ANC that’s barely there, Philips has implemented a system that is good enough for most. I am pleased with the ANC and will use these phones when I travel next.

The ANC function on these phones can be turned off if desired. There is also a special “awareness mode” that is an in-between mode that doesn’t completely turn off ANC but allows more environmental noise in, and this mode is really designed for permitting conversation without having to turn everything off completely. It works fairly well though the noise this mode produces via the external microphone is slightly harsh and shrill.

The default sound profile is not exactly perfect but it is better than many I have used and heard. These do boost the bass by default though not to an uncomfortable level. Bass boost is very common in headphones and it’s often too aggressive, but these actually give a modest boost. The midrange is a little soft though present. The highs sound bright and clear but not piercing. As a result, the sound profile is not quite perfectly balanced but it still good.

The sound profile can be tweaked via an app. I found the Philips Headphones app, installed it and started messing with it. The app works better than the reviews have suggested and it does a decent job of adjusting the headphones on the fly. The mode can be changed as well as the sound profile to adjust for different could quality based on music type, and there is a custom setting so that the equalizer can be adjusted to taste. The only complaint I have with the app is that there is about a 1s pause when changing modes between ANC. Awareness mode and Off, though this gap does not occur when changing the mode via the button on the headphones.

I like these ANC phones. They’re not perfect but they’re better than average with a good ANC function and decent sound. The have absolutely incredible connectivity, and they can be adjusted to taste via an app. This is a pair to keep on the short list if you need Bluethooth headphones that maintain a connection a long way from the source and provide ANC in the deal.

I have worked with a lot of different headphones, mostly active noise canceling (ANC) phones but also more traditional phones. Over the years I have had several Sennheiser phones and they typically have balanced sound and good build quality. This set is a step down from many of the others with which I have worked, though they’re still decent.

My preference on headphones is over-the-ear phones which for me are more comfortable. These particular phones are on-ear, and these pinch a little after extended wear. They’re better than some of the other on-ear phones with which I have worked, but I still prefer over-the-ear phones. One preference I have is a headphone that clamps down fairly tightly when worn so they’re less likely to slip off when I tilt my head down; these are a lighter fit.

These are Bluetooth-only phones and as such cannot be used with non-BT devices. This is unfortunate but isn’t a deal-breaker. These connect easily and quickly.

These are not ANC phones, but they have excellent passive noise canceling which is quite surprising for on-ear phones. They reduce ambient noise in my office considerably, which us especially noticeable when running a large fan that I use to generate white noise. I am pleased with that aspect of these phones. These are still not as effective as a set of ANC phones.

The sound profile is fairly typical of Sennheiser phones, though the bass is mildly beefed up.. The trend with phones these days is overdriven bass, and these do increase the bass response a little bit but not to a headache-inducing level. The midrange is full and warm, and that’s a good thing as many times the increased bass comes at the expense of the midrange. The highs are bright and clear without being piercing. Overall, the sound is reasonably balanced, but certainly not audiophile quality.

Build-wise, these actually feel a bit on the cheaper side which is surprising. These aren’t exactly fragile, but they are definitely not of the same build quality as other Sennheisers I have used in the past.

These are probably best described as entry-level headphones. They’re not the highest quality, and they are not the most sturdy, but the sound quality is fine and the cost is right. The main thing I would change is the addition of an audio port so they could be used as wired phones.

I have worked with numerous pairs of active noise canceling (ANC phones) and I’ve seen a wide variation in sound profiles, features, and the quality of the ANC function. Some are better than others. I was a bit skeptical of these because of the price; most of the ANC phones I have used that were worth anything have a higher price tag. These are better than the price suggests.

Right out of the box, these headphones do not draw much attention to themselves. They’re not flashy and do not have any noticeable markings on them unless you’re looking for them. They are over-the-ear headphones which tend to be more comfortable than on-ear phones, and these have a snug fit without clamping down tightly. They adjust easily to fit almost any size head too. The padding on the cans is soft enough to not pinch, though after extended wear they do start to get a little warm.

Pairing and connection with my computer was a painless affair and these were ready very quickly after they were powered on.

The ANC function is far and away better than any other headphones I have worked with in this price range. They’re almost as aggressive as that of the Bose QC-15’s that I own, without that weird faux pressure sensation when the ANC is turned on. Even with the volume down low, these cancel out enough background noise to make them a serious contender. I have no complaints with the ANC.

The sound quality is very good, though not quite to my tastes. The bass is very strong – much stronger than I like personally, but not out of line with what has been trending in the last decade. Where Skullcandy got it right, though, is in how well they’ve implemented the bass enhancement. Even though the bass is very strong (enough to give me a headache at higher volumes), it does not distort or turn into just low-frequency noise. More importantly, the bass enhancement does not stomp on the midrange which is the usual casualty. The midrange is warm and fairly balanced. The highs are bright and clear without being piercing. The end result is a sound profile that sounds full and rich. So many headphones with enhanced bass I have used have killed the midrange which makes music sound hollow, or distort the bass so much as to make music sound like a low-fidelity render. These are refreshing in that regard.

Some headphones detect when you take them off and pause music or playback when you take them off. These do not.

These come in a carry pouch that offers little in the way of drop and crush protection but it does keep them clean and free of scuffs and scratches. Also included is an audio cable for wired use as well as a USB Type C cable for charging.

Overall, these are far and away better than the price would suggest. They are very comfortable to wear, they have a good sound profile (particularly if you like heavy bass) and the ANC function is better than average and competitive with much more expensive headphones. These are budget-friendly ANC headphones with higher-end performance.

Note: There is more than one product attached to this listing. I am specifically reviewing the 18” light.

One of the things I have been researching for a while is ring lights. I have wanted one for a little while, but not the kind that sits on a desk and is only useful for making personal videos for upload. I wanted one that would be suitable for taking portrait photos and would be suitable for professional use. This is a nice ring light to that end and so far I am pleased with it, though I have not been using it long.

This is a large light, 18” in diameter which makes it quite a bit larger than most ring lights available right now. It is large enough that you can shoot photos or video through it using a full-sized camera with little effort, which is what I was looking for. It comes with a full-sized tripod (which it needs) as well as a nylon carry bag. It also comes with a mounting makeup mirror in the bag which is something I will not use with the ring light (I have other uses for it). In includes all of the hardware you need for mounting your camera, video camera or phone if you are a vlogger or content maker.

The very first thing I did with this light was point my camera right at it while using the electronic shutter, in order to determine if the LEDs in this light are strobing or not. I half expected these to strobe based on the price, but they do not which is a very good thing. It means steady, consistent light that does not flicker.

There are two adjustment knobs that are on the light assembly, one to control the brightness and the other to control the light temperature. The temperature range (speaking in generalized, observable terms rather than technical terms with numbers) allows for setting the light from an orangy golden-hour glow to a piercing frosty blue, and everywhere in between. So, though it may require some messing it allows for getting the light temperature just right based on skin tone and background. The brightness can be varied from a soft glow to bright enough to hurt your eyes when looking right at the ring. Thought not designed for such, this would work as a studio light in a pinch...

I do not have a light meter to check the actual light temperature or the lumens/lux output.

There’s a plastic cover over the LED array that helps to diffuse the lights and make them easier to face when using the light to illuminate a face for portraits.

The power source is AC 110/120. Some ring lights I have seen and used have USB-based power input instead. These tend to be smaller and less powerful.

Construction is good though I would stop short of saying it is solid and rugged. It is mostly plastic so it does have some flex to it but seems sturdy enough to handle getting moved around and jostled some. Because the housing is plastic instead of metal this is a lightweight unit and is easy to transport. This is a trade-off I have seen with tripods as well – lightweight for travel, heavier for less mobile work. This light seems geared for the traveler based on that.

Overall, I am pleased with this light. It is a bit better than I expected and it has everything you need in the package to be suitable for vlogging or studio use. It’s a big light so it does cost a bit more than a lot of the smaller, USB-powered lights out there but the cost is reasonable. If you’re looking for a ring light that can be used for either video content or of portrait work, give this one some consideration.

Most of the headphones with which I have worked have been active noise canceling (ANC) phones which have their strengths and weaknesses. I have a few pairs of nice non-ANC phones, some of which are excellent for studio work, but this is my first pair of true studio phones. After working with them, I am very pleased with them. They are comfortable to wear for long periods of time and they sound great with a very balanced sound profile.

These are over-the-ear phones, not on-ear, and I prefer that. They do not pinch or press my ears and I can wear them for several hours without them getting uncomfortable. The pads are soft and do not irritate as some phone pads sometimes can. The pads do not breathe, though, so after some time they do eventually get a bit warm.

If using these as Bluetooth phones, operation is simple – turn them on. They’re immediately ready to pair and my system discovered them and paired without incident. The Bluetooth range is good and I was able to get between 30’ and 50’ with walls in between before the sound began to stutter a little.

If you prefer to use them corded, that works too and these come with several audio cords with which to connect. Speaking of the cords: these do not use a standard audio cable with a standard connector on the phone side, so you can’t simply use any audio cable with them (though they will work with extension cables). Bear this in mind.

Volume can be controlled by touching the connector on the left side – flick up to increase volume, flick down to decrease.

The most important aspect of any headphones is the sound quality and these definitely deliver. The highs are sharp and crisp without being piercing. The midlevels are full and warm, and the base is strong without being overdriven. Most headphones anymore are tuned to overdrive the bass at the expense of the midrange making music sound hollow while pounding the listener to a headache. It is refreshing to listen to music that is properly balanced without needing an equalizer to get the sound right. I would not call these audiophile phones, but they’re better than many headphones I have used that cost much more.

If I could change one thing… I prefer a headphone set that clamps down on my head and fits snugly. These are not as snug as I’d like, but they are better than some I have used. When I turn my head and look down, they remain in place without slipping which is an issue with loose-fitting phones. Since these don’t slip, I’m satisfied.

I’m happy with these phones and based on my experience with them I am pleased to recommend them. They sound great and they are comfortable enough for extended use.

I have worked with GPS navigators from several manufacturers, including Garmin, Magellan and TomTom. Each unit has its strengths and weaknesses. My favorite GPS unit up this point has been another TomTom, an old Start 40 which served me well for several years. I was interested to see how much the series has changed since I got that older model. It has changed quite a bit – more than I expected. I like this navigator, though I can see a few things I’d change.

First off, I have the 6” model which is a beast. I am used to a 5” GPS which I have been using, and it took some time to adjust to the larger screen. This is not to say it bothers me; it just is enough of a difference to require getting used to it. If you are upsizing like that, be aware that it takes up more physical space and placing on the windshield might require replanning.

Out of the box, I powered it on, connected it to my WiFi network and downloaded over 6GB of updates. That’s a huge update. The map it holds is obviously the largest component to be updated, and it covers all of the US, Canada and Mexico. While it is nice to have all that coverage, I personally do not need that much map and would have liked the option of only having the US map on-board. That would cut memory requirements. My older model was limited in memory and the map grew until it could no longer fit; I can see the potential for that happening again.

For navigation, up to this point I have stuck with the default settings, except with the 2D/3D map setting.

My first trip with this unit was to work. I did not use it to navigate, I only used to to show the map as I drove. It found my fix quickly (one of the reasons I like TomTom navigators) and when I was driving it updated the map smoothly and quickly as I reached new features. It displayed road names, it showed the placement of certain POIs like gas stations, and because I was driving at sunrise the map switched from night mode to daytime so I got to see both maps.

I’ll state for the record, I am not fan of the daytime map’s default color scheme. I almost always use the 2D map, not the 3D one, and it uses a set of pastel colors that might be somewhat soothing on the eyes but they’re quite drab. I’d rather see a bolder map that makes features stand out more. Another thing this unit does not show is road symbols like the interstate shield, instead opting for just small-print words. I can live with that but I do prefer the symbols.

On the way home from work, I used the unit again, but this time to guide me on an alternate route. Friday afternoon traffic in this area is typically awful, and the route home is almost always snarled by at least one accident (sometimes as many as 4-5). I chose to follow a route I knew would take two hours to get home, though it moves the whole time. I loaded the first point into the GPS and it dutifully guided me there, taking me on a fairly optimal route. When I got there, I then told it to take me home and I was quite surprised – every other GPS unit I have used has tried to make me take a U-turn to go back the way I came to get back on the interstate (the source of the problem), but this one did not, instead taking me on a route that would connect me back to the interstate about 20 miles south. Knowing this was also a bad route traffic-wise, I made a planned turn in the middle of the route, skipping another 20 miles of interstate. Instead of insisting I turn around, the unit again adjusted my route and took me on almost the exact route I had planned to take anyway.

What impressed me is how quickly the unit rerouted me without trying to put me back on the original route it chose. This is quite different from most units. Normally I get “turn around when possible” or “recalculating” over and over – not this time.

I finally did let it put me on the interstate, about 5 miles from home. When I reached my exit is showed very clearly what lane it wanted me to use, and it was very obvious when I was to turn.

I use the American female voice that reads street names. She enunciates very clearly and is easy to understand. Many GPS units sound tinny or have a buzz when the voice is active, but this one does not. My old Start 40 sounded clear too and did not buzz. I think perhaps TomTom does a better job with designing their units for sound.

One thing I use my GPS for is speed tracking. When in an area where there are no posted speed limit signs, it is nice when the GPS shows the speed limit and your current speed. For this one, though, the speed display is very small. It’s out of the way which is good, but I’d prefer a larger display or at least some ability to make it bigger. If there is a setting for that I have not uncovered it yet.

My primary complaint with this GPS is actually the menu system, which I find to be very clunky and odd. I don’t like it, and preferred the older menu system. It is workable, regardless.

Most GPS units that offered traffic do so through a special antenna or attachment in the power connector. Rather than offer this, this unit instead gets traffic updates via your phone through a Bluetooth connection. This is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it does not require that the unit be plugged in all the time and it becomes much more portable. On the other hand, it means that it pulls data and if you’re in an area where there is no data connectivity your updates aren’t available. I’m still deciding if I like this arrangement or not.

This is a good GPS with a little room for improvement in a few areas. The screen real estate is nice, and it navigates very well (better than most others I have used). It enunciates clearly and updates en route smoothly and quickly. The menu system is a little clunky, and there are some display settings I think could be better. Overall, though, this unit gets the important things right. It’s a good unit at a competitive price.

I have worked with a lot of active noise canceling (ANC) headphones, from a large variety of manufacturers. Every set I have owned, from the top-of-the-line to the weakest and cheapest, has had its strengths and weaknesses. Until recently, Bose was the one to beat when it specifically came to the ANC function, though many others have a better sound profile. My favorite ANC phones are a set of Sony in-ear buds that rival Bose in ANC and trounce them in sound quality. When I found out that Microsoft had made an ANC headphone as well I did not have the highest of expectations – I expected mediocrity with the ANC and a reasonably good sound profile. I was dead wrong in both presuppositions – these are incredible headphones and are worth every penny of the asking price. They’re not absolutely perfect, but they’re better than one could reasonably expect.

I’ll start by saying that I am sorry in advance for the lengthy review. I have a lot to say on these, and I would much rather give far too much information than not enough. The present asking price as I write this is $349 and that’s a lot of money to drop, so more information is better.

Right out of the box these are relatively nondescript and don’t jump out as either flashy or gaudy. The controls that are visible and obvious are limited – a power button and a mute button, as well as the USB Type C power jack and a 3.5mm audio input jack. There are more controls, though, and it takes a quick glance at the documentation to get a feel for what’s there. There are two dials, one on each can, for controlling the level of ANC and for controlling the volume, L and R respectively. The flat portion of the cans facing outward are multi-function touch controls that allow you to play/pause, skip forward and backward, handle calls and also interact with your digital assistant. I will come back to that last point a little farther down.

I powered these on and they immediately announced that they were ready to pair. I paired them to my iPhone and they connected and were usable quickly, faster than most Bluetooth devices I have used. I put them on, tapped once on the right ear and Pandora immediately started up. That was easy!

The sound quality is very good though I will stop short of calling it audiophile level. The bass is good and not overdriven. I don’t care for deep, pounding bass and that is a problem with a lot of ANC phones I have used (Dre Beats being among the most aggressive in that regard). It softens as the volume level is dropped and that is very normal. The midrange is actually quite good with the proper amount of depth, so music sounds full and warm and not like it’s being piped through a tunnel. The highs are bright and clear though not piercing. Overall, these are among the most balanced ANC headphones when it comes to the sound profile. I cranked the volume and they don’t distort.

The ability to adjust the ANC is not new; however, the way these headphones do it is very innovative and unlike anything else I have seen. The dial that controls it gradually lessens the amount of ANC that is applied when listening, in small but perceivable steps, until the ANC is turned off. With the central air on in the house, I gradually went from no ANC to maximum and it very gradually wiped out all of that sound. When at the maximum level the ANC is almost as aggressive as Bose, with a lot less of the the weird pressure sensation on the ears.

A unique feature of these phones is integration with Cortana. When paired to a device running Cortana, simply saying “Hey, Cortana” gets its attention and you can interact with the same types of commands you use on the command line or the search window. It does require that Cortana be properly configured. I have Cortana installed on my iPhone (yes, you can do that and it works well), and the integration with the headphones when connected is good. I had a Windows Phone when they were still available and I would have liked to try this with that phone.

There’s some debate on whether these are on-ear or over-the-ear phones. These are very definitely over-the-ear phones unless your ears are huge. The cups are buttery soft as is the head band, and these are very comfortable. I am able to wear them for long periods of time without fatigue. They do get warm after a while, so keep this in mind.

One area a lot of headphones skimp on is the carrying case. The case with these phones is better than average. It is crush resistant and provides good protection for the phones. Included within is an audio cable for input as well as a USB charging cable.

These headphones bring a lot to the table and were quite a shock for me. I had much lower expectations, for the ANC function in particular but also for the sound profile. Both exceeded my expectations and the comfort factor is the cherry on top. These are excellent phones and I am very pleased with them.

I use active noise canceling (ANC) headphones all the time and prefer them to normal headphones as I tend to work in noisy environments and I’ve found that with ANC engaged I can play music at lower volumes. I like Sony headphones so I was excited to try these ANC ear buds. They’re a bit unusual in a few ways but they work well and are worth their asking price.

These are truly wireless and have no physical connection between them. Power them both on and they find one another. They pair via Bluetooth to a phone, tablet or PC, and the connection is stable up to about 40’ around corners. This is a good start.

There are several modes to these when it comes to the ANC function and each has its uses. I usually just use full ANC without any of the ambient sound modes turned on as it gives the best music experience. One of the two ambient modes is optimized for speech and voice, the other for more generalized noise. Neither completely cut off noise canceling, but rather they allow different bands of outside noise to come through. In full ANC mode, these are good noise cancellers, though not as aggressive as some others like Bose.

These have proven to be comfortable, and they have the little wings on each bud for keeping them in place in your ear. I used them while working in the yard and never once did I have a problem with slipping or falling out, even though I have the wrong size silicone insert on one of them.

The sound is very good but I would stop short of calling it outstanding. The bass is heavier than I like though not so bad that it gives me a headache unless I pump the volume up too much. The midrange is warm and full, and the highs are bright and crisp without being piercing. The sound can be adjusted a bit in the app that you can download, as it has an equalizer of sorts that lets you tweak the levels or choose a preset.

Ah, the app… This is the primary downside of these. The method to adjust these is either an Android or iOS app, not a physical piece of hardware and there is no Windows equivalent (for those who want to use these with a PC). The app is a little clunky though fairly self-explanatory and it does do what it’s supposed to do. Given a choice between an app or an additional piece of hardware, I would choose the hardware.

These charge up in the carrying case, which has leads that connect to each bud. Pay attention when you put these in the case – it is possible to reverse them, and while it hurts nothing the charging doesn’t work well… The case has some sort of battery in it and it charges the buds without being plugged in itself, though it does require occasional charging. Charging is fast – I charged them from empty to full in about an hour. One thing that could be improved, though: the buds can be popped in the charger while still powered on, and the act of charging them does not make them cut off. So, you can end up with dead buds and a dead charger too.

These are decent wireless sport buds that have good sound and good ANC functions. They’re comfortable and not overpriced. There are a couple of areas for improvement, particularly in charging but also in the app control, that would make these even better.

I will start by saying that I am typically not a fan of ear buds. I will also say that the very best headphones I have is a set of Sony active noise canceling ear buds. I have always had good success with Sony audio products and I regard the brand as an upper mid-range line. These buds are disappointing in that, while they’re comfortable for ear buds, the sound profile is lacking, specifically in the midrange.

This is a basic set of ear buds that work as you might expect. They do not have ANC functionality, there is no battery or battery pack and there is no Bluetooth functionality. These are straight plug-in audio gear with no fancy features. These will work with just about any device that provides a 3.5mm audio jack.

Most ear buds are uncomfortable to me, but these are surprisingly comfortable and I can wear these for a good bit of time. They come with several inserts of varying sizes so you can find the size that fits your ear canal just right. The included inserts are soft and do not irritate my ears as much as others have done in the past. I still very much prefer over-the-ear headphones which is a personal preference more than anything.

So, where’s the problem? The problem lies in the sound profile which is unbalanced. Having used literally dozens of sets of ear buds and headphones over the past 3-5 years I have developed a good feel for what sounds right and what doesn’t. Most ear buds have one of two issues, either way too much bass or almost none at all. These are surprising in that they actually get the bass just about right, not too heavy and not too light. The highs are very bright and clear, perhaps a touch too piercing for my tastes but not to the point of being unacceptable. The midrange, though, is flat. The result is that music sounds somewhat sterile and lackluster. This is similar to the issue I have seen with my Bose headset. These still sound good, but they fall short of where they could and should be.

Normally I would rate ear buds with a glitch in the sound profile a little higher, as they’re still quite usable and they sound decent. But, these are much more expensive than the average and I have heard less expensive buds with more balanced sound. Sony makes a number of sets of ear buds and headphones, but these are not among their best offerings.

I am usually not a fan of ear bud-style headphones as I have trouble finding sets that are either comfortable or have good sound. More often than not, buds have been tuned to have the bass either too strong or too weak and they sound very unnatural. Sony did a good job with these and got them sounding very balanced. They’re not perfect when it comes to comfort but there are ways to remedy this.

These are not active noise canceling (ANC) phones. Sony offers another model that is ANC-capable and they’re excellent but an order of magnitude more expensive. If you need ANC, this particular set of buds cannot do that so consider other options but be prepared to spend more.

These are sport-style ear buds in that they come on a neck harness and they are wireless. They connect easily via Bluetooth though they come with an adapter so they can be corded and used with devices that cannot work with Bluetooth. One concern with this type of phone is that often the cord is a little short between the harness and the buds, meaning a turn of the head pulls the cord a bit and can dislodge the buds from your ears. This particular set has some extra play in the cord so I have not had this issue as of yet. The cord on either bud can be “shortened” on either side by pulling the slack through tensors on the harness to reduce play in the wire.

In terms of use for sports and exercise, these feel a bit more fragile than most and I would caution against using them for doing anything much more active than running. They might hold up just fine, but these are a bit more pricey than most and are not ruggedized. This is probably my main complaint with these.

Comfort-wise, these are not bad. I have had better success with these than most, though I still greatly prefer over-the-ear headphones most of the time. The inserts are relatively soft and pliable and they do fit well, and the set comes with multiple sizes so adjustments can be made to get them to fit just right. In researching, I found that there are plenty of replacement tips; so, they can be swapped out if need be to find something that fits better or is more comfortable.

The main consideration about any set of phones, regardless of price, is the sound. In my mind, Sony has always had good quality products that do a fine job of balancing the sound. These ear buds are very much in line with my previous experiences. The sound profile is very balanced and even and the result is natural sounding playback. The tendency with the majority of manufacturers is to heavily push the bass. The bass in these is present and you can definitely hear it but it is not so pronounced as to dampen or overpower the rest of the profile. The midrange sounds good (particularly for ear buds) and had the right depth, meaning music sounds warm and not like it’s coming out of a tunnel or barrel. The highs are bright and clear but not piercing. I would stop short of saying these are audiophile quality, but the sound is much better than most bud-style earphones.

These are not your typical, cheap set of ear buds. These are better than the average and they are designed to be more comfortable and useful in an active lifestyle. They sound great. My only complaint is the construction - the harness in particular feels fragile. If you don’t need ANC and you don’t anticipate using your phones for heavy physical activity, these are a great choice. If you need something a bit more rugged, you might consider other options.

Most of my experience with Logitech products has been with keyboards and mice, though the company has made products in other segments as well, such as video surveillance systems and Modula-2 compilers. This is the first set of Logitech speakers I have tried and used, and I was expecting them to be a solid mid-range offering. They’ve proven to be better than that.

These speakers are not very large, about as big around as the lid on a container of oatmeal. They’re heavy, though, and in addition to the main speaker they have a bass subwoofer on each. They feel very solid and should hold up under some abuse shy of being dropped on a concrete surface.

My first test was to connect them to my phone via Bluetooth. I plugged them in, turned them on and they immediately started broadcasting their ID. My phone immediately saw them and I was able to pair and connect them without any issue at all. Based on my experience there, the Bluetooth connectivity is excellent. I later tried to connect them to my computer by the audio cable – simple and easy as should be expected.

The main question when using a set of speakers – how do they sound? In a word: excellent. The bass response is solid but not overdriven, the midrange is warm and has good depth, and the highs are sharp and clear without being shrill. I was expecting a more subdued sound profile, but Logitech did a good job with getting these to sound great. I would stop short of calling these audiophile quality, but the large majority of users should be happy.

I bumped up the volume and tried to get these to distort and I was unsuccessful. They remained clear even through the full volume range. I set them in the kitchen, turned up the volume and went to the basement as I was still able to hear the sound clearly – through the ceiling.

I do have speakers that sound better by a little bit, but they cost three times as much and they’re quite a bit larger. Considering the price point and the size of these speakers, these are much better than one could realistically expect.

I have used active noise canceling (ANC) headphones for many years and I have come to expect - and look for - the subtle differences between them. I have worked with ANC phones from Bose, Sennheiser, Monster, Noontec and quite a few more. All of them have their strengths and weaknesses. This is my first experience with Sony ANC phones, and I anticipated good ANC functionality and a solid sound profile. At the price point ($300 as I write this) they need to be excellent to be worth any kind of consideration. These were a huge shock to me: the ANC is nearly on par with Bose and the sound profile is solid, giving better results than I imagined.

I will address the ANC function first, then the sound profile, and afterward I will discuss design and features. I apologize ahead of time for being long-winded, but I’d rather give too much feedback than not enough.

The ANC function is, in a single word, outstanding. Bose is the standard by which I compare others and very, very few headphones get anywhere near the same level of noise cancellation as my Bose sets (QC-15 and QC-20i, by the way). Those that get close usually have the same weird pressure sensation for which Bose is known. My primary test is a loud fan that I use for generating white noise when I want to drown out everything around me at night. I turned the fan on high speed, plugged the Sony’s buds into my ears and turned them on. I put them in ANC mode and the fan all but disappeared. All that remained of the noise was a faint, higher-frequency hiss (distinct from the ANC hiss which I will explain later). Of all the phones I have used, this set and the Bose are the only ones to wipe out that much noise. I also went into the bathroom and turned on the ventilation fan to test, and these phones again wiped out a large majority of the fan noise. For this fan, the Bose sets have a very slight edge but you have to be looking for it to notice.

The main difference between the Bose sets and these is the utter lack of that weird pressure sensation with these. If you don’t like that sensation but you want very high ANC, these are simply excellent. Like a lot of ANC phones, these generate a faint hiss that you really won’t notice unless you’re not feeding any sound at all to them and you’re listening for it.

The sound profile is also quite solid. Usually with ANC phones, because of the cancellation of certain bandwidths the phones compensate by twiddling the sound profile to fill in what was dropped, and usually this means overcompensation in the bass range (if you use Dre Beats, you know exactly what I mean). Heavy bass gives me headaches so I avoid headphones where the bass has been given too much boost. With these, Sony did not overdrive the bass at all but it’s still very solid and full - love it. The midrange is very warm and rich and music has the right depth. The highs are very bright and clear but not piercing. Overall, I am very pleased with the sound profile - not audiophile quality but closer than most.

In terms of design, these are a wireless earbud product with a neck harness. So, these are neither on-ear or over-ear phones. The harness and slack but adjustable wiring to the actual earbuds ensures that they can be set up so they won’t tug or pull when you’re working out, running or otherwise doing physical activity. Being wireless, there’s no cord to tangle up either. And, one size really does fit all which is a problem with some regular phones. The neck assembly has a leatherette padding that is soft and will not chafe.

The Bluetooth functionality works great. I paired these to my phone and they paired and connected in less than 5 seconds which is really all I could ask. After a full power-off, I turned them back on and they immediately connected to my phone again. I have no complaints there.

One of the really interesting features of these is the ability to turn off the ANC and use them without any cancellation, but they have another unusual mode that I have only seen in one other pair of phones - they have an “ambient sound” mode that you can turn on that dampens the feed in the buds and slightly increases the surrounding noise without turning off the ANC. Assuming the volume is not turned up too loud, this allows for carrying on a conversation without turning off the feed. I will say, though, that listening to my own voice coming through in this mode is disconcerting.

I do not know yet how long the battery in these lasts. So far I have not run them all the way down.

Included in the box are the phones themselves, a conversion cable so that they can be used with an audio jack (handy when Bluetooth is not an option), a cable for charging, an in-flight audio adapter, several silicone tips fo the buds so you can get the size right, and a protective carry bag.

The carry bag is the only complaint I have with the whole package - it offers little protection from drops and crushes. If you only are concerned about keeping everything together and keeping the set very clean, the bag is acceptable, but if you need better protection that consider getting a third-party hard case or use the original packaging box.

Sony got these right and even at the price tag these are easy to recommend. They’re comfortable (more comfortable than I expected for ear buds), they have excellent sound and the ANC function is outstanding. I prefer these to my Bose phones and will be using these instead.

I have worked with a lot of headphones, active noise canceling (ANC) phones in particular. ANC phones are interesting in that while they are good at stripping out white noise they frequently do not sound quite right because they twiddle the sound profile, usually in the bass range, to compensate for the sound frequencies they filter out. Also, there are varying levels of ANC, the standard to which others are compared is Bose. This headset by Jabra came as a huge shock to me, both for the very balanced sound profile and the aggressive ANC function.

This headset is on-ear, not over-the-ear. Usually I am a bit wary of on-ear headphones as they tend to be a little uncomfortable. These have very soft, leather-like pads and they are actually quite nice – for a while. After about an our of wear they start to get slightly uncomfortable for me, though taking them and shifting them a little makes them fine again.

The ANC function is VERY aggressive, approaching the same level as Bose but not quite. It is able to wipe out the sounds of the A/C, a fan, engine noise and more. Like Bose, when these are first turned on the ANC gives the wearer a sensation of pressure on the ears. Using this without feeding in noise, it is possible to enjoy relative quiet when traveling, reading, studying or enjoying similar activities.

The sound profile is on point. The bass is present and unmistakable, but it is not pushed forward so much as to dominate the whole profile and drown out the midrange. The midrange is bright and warm, giving music the right depth instead of making it sound like it’s either in a tunnel or in a barrel. The highs are very good – solid but not piercing. Jabra has nailed the sound profile where a lot of others have screwed up.

This is also a headset for talking, and call clarity when using with a mobile phone is very good. I have had excellent results using this headset and it has worked extremely well for me. There is a caveat, though – because this headset covers both ears, it is not suitable for use while driving in many jurisdictions. It’s great when in the office, but know your local and state laws if you plan to use it in a motor vehicle.

There are two ways to use this headset and connect it. It has built-in Bluetooth and it pairs and connects very quickly with my phone. It also has a USB dongle for connecting to a PC, though it can be connected to the PC via Bluetooth too. My observation there is that volume levels are reduced when connecting to a PC via Bluetooth.

The headset comes in a crush-resistant case and includes the USB dongle and a USB cable for charging.

I can find little about which to complain with this headset. It does get slightly uncomfortable for extended wear, but it has great ANC and a very balanced sound profile. As a headset it works great for talking, too, and the Bluetooth pairing is fast. This has already become my favorite set of headphones for streaming music, though because of laws where I live I cannot use it as a hands-free set while driving.

[[VIDEOID:99ec24b728fa83828f854618bef8cc0]] Most of the Bluetooth speakers I have used have been smaller and more portable, designed to be on-the-go and useful when traveling or outdoors. This speaker by GGMM is also wireless and can go with you, but I personally prefer to keep it in my room above my desk where I can use it to listen to music. This is a much better speaker than most of the speakers I have used and I am very pleased with it.

This is a large speaker, bigger than most I have used and as a result it weighs more. It is encased in a leather cover and looks very upscale when compared to plastic or rubber. The controls are straightforward and easy – power on/off, set the mode between Bluetooth, WiFi and Line-in, volume up and down and finally a bass booster. On the back there is a barrel port of plugging in the speaker, a reset button that you likely will never need to use and the port for plugging in a 3.5mm plug.

The sound profile is about as close to perfect as I have seen in any speaker. The bass is on target – strong but not overdriven unless you use the bass booster. The midrange is excellent and the music sounds rich and full, not lifeless, hollow or like it’s coming from a tunnel. The highs are bright and clean but not piercing. The sound is balanced very well and I am happy.

The bass booster does exactly what you think it does – it gives the bass a kick. Even with the boost, the bass is not overpowering but it comes forward quite a bit on bass-heavy tracks. I do not use the bass boost often as I prefer the highs.

So far I have had no connection issues and the speaker connects very quickly when put in Bluetooth mode.

This is an excellent speaker – far and away better than most smaller speakers I have seen and used. It is much more expensive, but it brings to the table great sound and fine connectivity. I use this in my home office where it sits just above eye level on my desk shelf, and I use it every night for listening to music.

Disclosure: I was provided a sample of this product in exchange for a fair, honest and thorough review. Even though I received this product at minimal or no cost I have rated and reviewed this product without bias, based solely on my experience with it.

This is my first exposure to Panasonic Active Noise Canceling (ANC) headphones. This particular model is very inexpensive relative to most ANC phones on the market, and unfortunately the low price is justified. These phones fall short in a couple of important areas.

First and foremost, these are ANC phones and the ANC function does indeed work. That said, the degree to which it works is in line with the pricing. I have a very specific fan in the house that I use as a benchmark, as most ANC phones are able to nearly completely wipe out the white noise that this fan generates when on the lowest speed setting. The Panasonic phones kill a good bit of the fan noise but allow more noise than almost every other ANC set I have tried. In the office I tried these phones in an area serviced by two large air handlers that generate a lot of noise and these headphones did remarkably well though still not as well as most other phones I have tried in the same environment. Now, when compared to the likes of Bose, Panasonic does a very poor job but then again they cost maybe 15% of what Bose costs. When considering this price differential the Panasonic phones do a decent job with their ANC which should be acceptable by most for traveling.

One area where these phones fail, though, is in build quality. These headphones are extremely lightweight and they feel very flimsy and fragile. These are not the headphones to take when traveling frequently. To add insult to injury, they come with a cloth carry bag which offers absolutely no protection at all beyond serving as a dust cover.

Worse, though, is the miserable sound quality. I don't know if my specific headset is the problem but while I have a decent full range of sound, everything across the spectrum sounds slightly tinny and hollow. I was encouraged that Panasonic does not overdrive the bass as many manufacturers tend to do and instead delivers a fairly balanced spectrum, but this does not make up for the poor quality of sound. As these are inexpensive headphones I would never expect them to be audiophile quality, but the sound should absolutely be much better than it is.

I was encouraged to see that Panasonic includes a 2-prong adapter in the package, but then they omit the 1/4" adapter which is something I actually use.

Panasonic has made a very inexpensive ANC headphone and unfortunately the low cost is justified. While the ANC capabilities are within reason for the price range, the sound quality and build quality are severely lacking. If looking for ANC phones for the purpose of using the ANC function, and keeping costs low is important, then these phones may fill that need acceptably. However, if sound quality is in any way important, these are the wrong phones and will sorely disappoint.

Perhaps if the sound was better, or if the price was lower, these would be great headphones. The design is slick, and actually comes fully black-gray brand new (I know they "customize" over the years, but the blue on the cans in the Amazon picture threw me off).
The stretchiness is great, and I don't fear that the headphones would break easily if, say, someone accidentally sat on them. Nonetheless, I do have some gripes.

First, the sound is absolutely awful for $100. There was some tinny noise, and because the headphones have a hard time adjusting to my skull, I couldn't get the right position for the full sound effect. It's a shame that headphones of this price can't even beat my $20 Sennheisers (which is no jab at my beloved Sennheisers). Another issue I had is with the cord. I understand that it's certainly non-tangable, but it comes with a longer cord that makes absolutely no sense. The longer cord isn't the major issue, though; it's the short cord that extends from the headphones: it's so short, it can't attach to *anything* without requiring the longer cord. Maybe if you were on your bed and the iPod/music device was on your chest it would work, but I imagine people aren't buying these cans for bed use. The longer cord is absolutely fundamental to using, so I don't know why they even bothered separating it from the cans themselves. They should've made the shorter cord longer and the longer cord slightly shorter.

While the design is superb, I'd look elsewhere if you want good sound quality.
I bought this product because it matched my black iPod classic but I returned it the same day. The speaker looks cool but the sound is horrible. It was tinny and muffled and not worth $60.
wonderful buy.  good protection.  multiple colors so you can tell one from the others right away.  lots less screeching arguments!!!!!!!!!!!!!
Works great. Installed immediately but the sound is kind of tinny. I can live with that. Excellent compliment to my Echo family.
Sound is tinny you could add a external speaker for better sound. Plug right in outlet no cord in the way.

We bought two of these in December 2015. Hooked each camera up. Downloaded the online app. Put in a memory card. Turned on our iPads, Phones, and Apples. Presto we could see every point inside our home should our exterior camera system connected to the home security device ever fail.

We travel 140 miles West to our 2nd home and watch inside our home, while driving whoever is not at the wheel will pull up the home-cam so we can see what is happening on our cell phones. We went to Vegas, a few months ago and hired a dog sitter to stay with our beloved pet at our home. We were able to check-in & from our hotel room, Freemont Street or the Strip and check on our home without any problems.

Unless you are still operating in the AOL age or have so many firewalls up the smoke detectors keep going off inside your home; I can't see why the product would not work for a person needing a quick install. The type of one they control that is portable enough to move from room to room, (even a window seal).

If you live in a valley surrounded by mountains where at best you have a fuzzy cell phone use, you may want to get the kind of cams able to be through DSL if possible. By the way, it is not just your computer that needs updates if you no longer use brick phones.
