These headphones don't really hit the mark for me -- maybe because I have a small head and smaller ears. They stay on and don't fall off even when running but I can't get the fit correct where the driver stays sealed in my ear the way its supposed to (tried all sets of tips included). When they come loose the sound quality is very bad since these are a sealed design headphone and rely on creating a seal with your inner ear to reproduce low frequencies, so they sound very tinny and harsh. Even when I use my fingers to hold the drivers in place though, the sound quality of these is pretty mediocre compared to my other sony BT headphones.

Also when I tighten the band in the back to prevent cable noise when running, that makes the control pod be on the back of my neck which is kind of awkward to use. I also don't like the overall design which looks and feels kind of bulky, at least they are pretty light weight though. These headphones worked as expected and had no issues with syncing, if they fit better I would have given them 3 or 4 stars but I have a pair of sony bluetooth headphones that sound better, fit better, and look better for about the same cost so I really can't recommend these.

I am actually quite impressed by this speaker.  I've had a few cheap Bluetooth speakers, but none have sounded as good as this one does.  I fully expected it to have a small, tinny sound.  It surprised me when it didn't.  Mind you, it doesn't have a big bassy sound either, but it is as good as a normal radio and much better than the speakers in most portable devices.  I would recommend this.

Works a little too well; listening to movies, streaming, YouTube. The louder you set the volume, the more static and tinny the sound. Keeping the volume low helps with sound quality. Does not always work well with some phone calls however. Caller sometimes hears lots if static. Overall, works in a pinch.

These earbuds are pretty good for this price level. The sound is smooth, not tinny like you usually get with cheap headphones. The sound is not as detailed as more expensive earbuds, though. There is enough bass for the acoustic music that I usually listen to, but it is not thumping like with some headphones. Higher frequencies are not as bright and clear as on more expensive earbuds.

There are a lot of different ear tips in the box. The pair that were pre-installed didn't give me very good sound quality, but different size/shaped ear tips (that were included) worked much better for me. If you're hearing weak bass, switching eartips can often fix that problem as well as improve comfort.

10 hour battery life is pretty good for lightweight earbuds like this; much better than the "true wireless" style of earbuds. Sound quality is also much better than "true wireless" earbuds in this price range.

Lightweight and water resistant makes these earbuds great for running and other workouts. Many earbuds are heavier and quickly become uncomfortable when I'm working out.

I like that a simple carrying case is included to keep these from getting tangled and broken when I'm carrying them in my gym bag.

These earbuds are cheap ($10) and look and feel like toys. Very lightweight all plastic exterior. I wasn't expecting much, but the sound is very good for this price level. At the moderate volumes that I like to use, the music does not sound distorted or tinny. Not as much detail as from a bigger heavier headphone, but this is fine for listening to MP3s on my cellphone when I'm jogging. The lightweight construction means it doesn't fall out of my ears as often as heavier earbuds. I have tried some of the other cheap bluetooth headphones from Amazon, and this is the best that I have used for under $10. It even uses one of the newer Bluetooth standards that shows headphone power level on my phone screen; as someone who is always worried about rechargeable devices running out of power, this is a really great feature. Unfortunately, battery life is somewhat less than the advertised 5 hours. Even at moderate volumes, I'm down to about 50% battery after an hour and a half. That's fine for a gym workout or a subway commute, but not for airline travel.

It comes packaged in a self-destructing pile of paper and plastic. I wish they had included a carrying case instead of all this garbage.

This is an excellent mid-priced medium-sized Bluetooth speaker. The speaker measures 9x3x3 inches and weighs 8 ounces (half a pound). Despite the moderate size, it does fill a medium sized room with great quality music. At medium volumes, the sound is very rich and well balanced. Sound starts to get a little tinny near maximum volume, but the distortion is tolerable, not painful like with cheap speakers. For the price, I think the sound is great. Volume is excellent for a speaker of this size. Sound quality is also excellent; probably the best I've heard for a speaker of this size. I do have some larger, more expensive speakers that sound better at high volumes, but I am very happy with this one for the size and price.

The "extra bass" button on the top of the speaker gives you a pronounced reverb effect which is fun for dance music, but maybe not something I want to use all the time.

This is the first bluetooth speaker that I have owned with built-in party lights on the front of the speaker. That's a cute feature if you're a group of lights at a party. I don't think the lights are synchronized with your music, however, which would be a more fun feature.

The speaker pairs easily with my Android phone (don't have an iphone to try). You can pair it directly with the Android bluetooth control or use the optional Sony SongPal app. The app gives you more features like syncing multiple speakers, a basic equalizer, control of the party lights on the front of the speaker, and a power-down timeout. Syncing multiple speakers would be great for increasing the volume and range of your music at an outdoor party. Some photos of the app are attached. The Sony SongPal Android app is a fairly large 44MB, but you don't need it for basic speaker use.

The manual doesn't say how big is the internal battery for this speaker, but it must be huge since they claim 24 hours of music playing. You can forget those days when bluetooth speakers had only 1 or 2 hours of battery life. There is even a USB-out port on this speaker so you can use the speaker battery to recharge your smartphone if you really need to.

Unfortunately, there is no carrying case included with this speaker. The speaker does have a scratch-resistant rubberized exterior and they claim IPX5 water resistance, so it work great for outdoor parties, even when the weather is iffy.

Most $10 headphones sound tinny. These actually sound decent. Not as accurate as $50 earbuds, but decent bass and good clarity in the midrange. These also come with much better accesories than other earbuds in this price range. The case is very useful and you get 5 pairs of ear tips to guarantee a comfortable and clear sounding fit. The wires are not thick and heavy like you get in a lot of better headphones, but heavy cables are a negative if you use the headphones for running since they uncomfortably bounce around. These cables are thick enough to reduce tangling problems, but not heavy enough to cause problems when exercising. I really can't complain about anything for the $10 price and you regularly can find these for $10 from various vendors, including Amazon at times.

I tried out two of these speakers, one in red and one in black. It has a lot of excellent features and functions:

*The red color is gorgeous, very bright and clear, and the black is deep and rich.
*The speaker can expand or contract, with a nice accordion feature. It needs to be open when you are using it, and you close it to pack it up to carry it around.
*It is rechargeable, so you don't have to worry about changing batteries. It takes only a couple of hours to charge and lasts up to 12 hours of play time.
*If you have more than one, you can hook them together and create a tiny, stereo system.
*It can hook up to your iPhone, PC, laptop, MP3 player and tablets--essentially anything that allows you to plug in earbuds.
*The sound quality is excellent for such a small speaker.
*There is a black, unpadded, cloth, drawstring bag to carry the speaker in.
*There is a audio/charging cable, and you can charge the speaker with a USB AC wall adapter or your PC.
*When the speaker is charging, the LED light on its bottom will glow red. When it is completely charged, it will glow blue.
*There is an on/off switch, an audio/charging input port, an audio-input jack, and a volume-control dial. Note that you have to turn on the volume both on the speaker and on the audio source you have it hooked to.
*This tiny speaker weighs less than 3 ounces.

I've personally used this speaker hooked up to my iPhone to listen to music through [[ASIN:B005V1N71W Pandora]], and to my [[ASIN:B002MAPSC6 MP3 player]] to listen to audiobooks. It works extremely well, and I'm delighted with it. My husband tested out this speaker, too, primarily with his iPhone, and he loves it as well. The sound quality is good, not tinny, but quite resonate, and I am able to turn the volume up high enough that I have to remember to turn it down late at night so as to not disturb my neighbors.

I have only two minor complaints: (1) The instructions provided are in such tiny print, I needed a magnifying glass to read them. (2) When I hook the speaker to my iPhone, its cable is so short, the speaker has to be unhooked before I can use the iPhone for any other purpose than to play an audio app. If the speaker's cable were were even six inches longer, that wouldn't be necessary and I could multitask on my iPhone a lot more efficiently while it is attached to this speaker.

Disclaimer: I was offered a sample of this product so that I could try it out in order to be able to write a review.

I see people raving up and down about the perfection and wonderfulness of these headphones; I’m not as completely blown away by them as those people are. Quality of construction does seem to be excellent (although because Amazon doesn’t lower all prices at the start of Prime Day but only lowers some of them well after Prime Day has begun, I had to send back the first pair I bought and purchase another pair to get a discounted price, and the piston things for extending and compressing the size of the headphones was smoother on the first pair I had) and they’re comfortable enough to wear for extended periods, but while it may be a limitation of Bluetooth (I don’t know), I haven’t noticed myself being amazed by their bass response. No, in fact I just now watched the video for Shake It Off and listened to a couple of Lana Del Rey tracks and these headphones are definitely lacking in bass response – as in, there’s very little, and what there is gets completely lost under any midrange and high-end sounds that may be playing at the same time. They’re tinny-sounding. I have to wonder what the people are listening to with these who are praising the sound quality so enthusiastically.

On the other hand, I don’t ordinarily listen to music anymore, but only to talks and lectures; While I’m watching movies is probably the only time I’m going to really want big bass, and I watched The Revenant last night and didn’t feel like I was missing anything…

So their construction is much more solid than that of probably most other headphones on the market, they’re comfortable to wear, and there’s a nice ecosystem of accessories out there, but I personally find the sound quality quite lacking and I’m going to have to decide whether to hang onto these or return them.

Absolutely love this monitor. I now have it next to my Acer GD235HZ (4+ years old) and the Asus makes it look lifeless. Yes, the Acer GD235HZ was great in its heyday, when NVidia was still cranking out the original 3D Vision (before light burst), so this was my monitor of choice back then. Over the years, I got into 3D sessions when I was in the mood, but short periods with an active shutter set up will tire your eyes out in no time, AND make you feel drugged. This is with a 120hz display mind you.

The colors on this Asus IPS screen are just so vivid -- text and graphics are super sharp! ! And in theater mode, the black is like velvet! The screen default is very bright, so during non-gaming periods, I tend to drop it down. The Asus monitor uses passive technology which means inexpensive 3D glasses (same as the theater gives out), and longer playing periods. I'll sacrifice the horizontal resolution loss, over expensive active shutters any day. If you sit at least three feet away from the monitor, the 3D looks amazing, unless your're one of these anal journalists who judge it from every angle. Yeah, when I play a game, I tend look directly into monitor, not off from the the side of my desk. If you want to watch a 3D movie with six people, then perhaps a living room, passive TV over 52" would fit the bill. The Asus VG23AH is a monitor, and one that sports a pretty vibrant, spectacular 3D picture if you know how to use it. There are a number of settings which can be tweaked, and if you do a google search, there is a very informative set up guide which is also posted on youtube. In addition to running native 3D programs through TriDef, there is a 2D-3D button right on the front panel. I've never seen this as a button-based feature, but it takes any 2D media and displays it in 3D. A number of TV sets have a similar option, but I've never seen it right in the hardware. The results may vary, but considering the original content is 2D, you'll be quite impressed.

As of now, I have my PC hooked up to it via DVI cable and tried a number of games, including Sonic Generations, the Half Life 2 series and mods, Skyrim, and others. All are breathtaking, but you do need drivers. I already had the TriDef drivers when I purchased it years back, but you will need to lay down $40-$50.00 for a licensed copy in order to take advantage of PC gaming.
I will also hook my PC up through HDMI and try the other modes of 3D like Side by Side, which will expand my capability with 3D content available on the web.

In addition to the PC, I have my PlayStation 3 plugged in through the extra HDMI port, and the PS3 automatically recognized the 3D display, when running a game that supports this feature. There are a good number of PS3 games in 3D and they look absolutely stunning on this monitor, especially the Zen Pinball series!

Oh, the sound through HDMI will come through the monitor's speakers, and it's pretty good actually! Not tinny like other monitors.

Overall, I'm loving this monitor -- once you see IPS you will be spoiled!

Note: I got this off of Amazon's warehouse deals for $191.00 (aka a steal for IPS + 3D, It was classified as "Used/Like New", but it looked brand new to me when it arrived. Everything was still wrapped in its originally manufacture's packaging. A totally worthwhile buying experience!

The size difference between 40 and 42 inches is more noticeable than what I thought it would be. My 40 inch tv does a noticeably better job of rendering from the satellite dish. Both televisions are excellent for over the air HD content, and the 42 inch tv, surprisingly, did a better job of connecting with my Mac Mini over a dvi-to-hdmi cable. Unlike the 40 inch, which is a newer model, the 42 inch gives full 1080p with no over-scaling.

The sound is where the 42 inch falls apart. Tinny, weak, and truly awful out of the box. I was able to get an acceptable sound for a bedroom tv (which is what I am using this for) by playing with the equalizer and presets (I set it to jazz and dynamic). I do not think it would work in a busier, louder room. For now, the picture and sound are enough better on the 40 inch that I have decided to keep that one as my living room tv (my living room is tiny), but the 42 inch is great in the bedroom.

I shopped around a long time before I bought the 40 inch tv, because I've got serious budget constraints, and I needed something I could afford AND that I wouldn't regret buying every time I tried to watch it. Now that I have both of these, I have to say that I still think the 40 inch is the better bargain with two "unlesses" - 1. Get the 42 inch if size really matters to you, and 2. Get the 42 inch if your primary video source is going to be 1080p dvi-to-hdmi (i.e. you have cut your cable and are using a computer as your main source of entertainment). If that's the case, you'll probably want to get a decent set of speakers to go along with this.

This came perilously close to being an angry review of Windows 8 the first week I had the 13, but then I calmed down, learned enough about how to navigate the new OS, and began to enjoy the computer for its own sake. It's a fast, powerful little number with a startlingly quick boot up, something I can't say for any of my other machines. It multi-tasks better than any computer I've ever owned, and I'm not just talking about having Chrome open with a couple of Word documents. I'm talking a couple of graphics-intensive programs plus Spotify, plus a web browser with a lot of open tabs. Basically a bunch of memory hogs couldn't even slow the 13 down, and I am loving that.

Why? Well I'm not a gamer per se, so what's important to me is that I can do the work I do -- I'm a writer, editor, and artist with a lot of social media outlets -- in the way I want to do it, which is often a matter of moving from one program to another, to work in a limited time frame. With music. The 13 can handle everything I throw at it including large graphics files, without a wibble. The games I do play play flawlessly and look terrific.

Specifics: The keyboard is fairly compact, and there's no number pad, which I miss only a little. It has a good feel, which is important for anyone who spends hours typing. The screen is small, obviously, but it's bright and crisp. Graphics look good on this screen, though I have noticed that color is rendered a bit differently than on my other laptops. I haven't tried adjusting it yet. Once I start printing out my art, I'll do any color adjustments I need to do. The sound? I love it. It's clear and warm, nothing tinny or muddy about these speakers.

It comes loaded with some decent software. There's not a lot of bloat here. What you get is useful or genuinely fun, like the Alien FX which tickles me because it allows me to change the lighting theme. Yes, yes, I know that's fru-fru stuff, but I like the shiny. Oh, and a terrabyte HD? I am so there. I have a lot of media files, and that lets me keep them all in one place rather than having to store them on an external hard drive. And speaking of drives, do be aware that there is no optical drive in this unit. If you need one you'll have to get a stand-alone. This isn't a huge hardship, they're not expensive these days. It's just a bit inconvenient.

Look, the bottom line here is that if you can afford a computer just for gaming you can probably afford something bigger and better. But if you also have to use your computer for other things, work, school, a life... this is going to serve you pretty well, in my opinion. If, like me, you want to do graphics work on a laptop (My desktop is ancient and creaky but up to this point was the only machine I had that could support Photoshop effectively.) this is a machine to consider.

This is not a bad clock radio for the price I paid. It's not a great one either, but it fit the profile of what I wanted with one exception, which I'll get to in a bit.

First off, it's smallish, which is a blessing on a crowded nightstand. The display seems fine to me, neither too bright, nor too dim. It's easy to program, thank goodness. I've had a lot of electronics that require three hands, and a stopwatch to be properly programmed. The ICF-C218 has a button or a dial for each function. Just follow the instructions and you'll be fine. It's a bit hard to see the radio dial unless you pick it up, but that's a minor thing for someone like me, who pretty much keeps it on one station. It's not programmable; you have to change the station with a tuning dial. However the reception is excellent, even without an external antenna.

My quibble, and it's a relatively small one, is that the sound is tinny. I don't expect a lot out of a small radio like this, but I have a Sangean which is even smaller, and the sound is much better. It's not a deal-breaker, I got what I wanted in every other respect.

Bottom line: Good price point for a basic clock radio with excellent reception, and so-so sound.

Good crisp audio quality for phone calls. I like an on-the-ear headset instead of in-ear because cell phones have little or no sidetone.

Don't know what sidetone is? Back in the day, land line phone handsets fed the sound from the mic back into the earpiece, so a person could clearly monitor their own voice (and also hear any other sounds that the other party could hear that the mic picked up). That enabled a person to modulate their own voice (instead of screeching in order to hear themselves) and speak much more clearly. It made for a much better phone conversation experience. That feature was called sidetone.

It's a feature that cell phone designers and engineers somehow decided not to add to cell phones, or to make it so low in volume as to be nonexistent.

So until either cell phone engineers put sidetone back into cell phones or headset manufacturers start building it in as a feature, the workaround is on-ear headsets that allow you to hear your own voice while you speak.

The downside is that on-ear headsets aren't exactly convenient to carry around, and they're not inconspicuous. And they can be a bother if you're wearing a hat.

But they do give you some natural sidetone by allowing you to hear the sound of your voice. And this headset from Logitech, as I said, has some good crisp audio quality for phone calls.

Which brings up another point. Even after years of development, possibly the thing cell phones still do worst is make phone calls. The audio can still be garbled and fluttery due to digitizing and signals that fade in and out in strength. So good audio quality---in that mid-range EQ sweet spot---can make cell phone calls a lot more pleasant.

While there's a volume control on the cord, there's no answer button. That's probably a decision to keep the headset compatible with many devices.

Overall, good headset.

I compared the Kindle 2 and this device for many months and also the nook when it came out. The pics of the Cabor Small Wireless Headphones looked like a couple other pairs I've owned, and I was looking for a new set, so I ordered them.

Unlike my other wrap-around outside ear headphones, these came coiled up. When I gently pulled them open and put them on, they shot off my head as they coiled back up. There's no way to stretch them out - they coil back up if you put them down. As a result, I find they're very fiddly to put on, and while I can get them on both ears so they don't come off, I couldn't run in them or do something active that involved leaning over repeatedly.

Soundwise, these were pretty good - not great, but definitely not bad. I didn't find the sound tinny or weird but pleasant, and very good for audiobooks. Overall this is an okay headset, but next time I'll buy a set that doesn't want to coil up every time you let go of it.

It's attractive, easy to use, a little heavier than the size would suggest, which is good as it isn't as easy to knock over, and the shape would make that challenging anyway as it's short as 2/3 of a soda can but is thicker. The buttons aren't a hassle to push.

I love this little speaker as I can finally have quality sound anywhere in my condo - no wires,. Thumbs up!

When our old sound bar died at the beginning of a Zoom meeting, I had to order a replacement immediately. I chose this 16 watt Saiyin based on price and reviews, and since our main concern was hearing others better in meetings, I wasn't worried about great sound quality.

But to my surprise, we're quite happy with this sound bar. First off, the controls are simple and easy to use - it's pretty much plug and play, it came with needed cables and it's not weird or ugly. It doesn't smell like chemicals or uncured plastic. And most important, it works and works well. It enhances the sound and volume on cheap or quiet computer speakers so you can easily hear what's being said, and the sound - which I was afraid would be tinny or shrill - was actually good for speaking. It's not as good for music unless you play it at lower levels, in which case it's not audiofile quality but sounds pretty good, too.

This sound bar was an unexpectedly good purchase. For our use - Zoom meetings, quiet music, maybe Youtube videos - it sounds better than my Creative Acoustics computer speakers with subwoofer and better than other external speakers and small sound bars we've used. It doesn't sound as good as our much larger soun bar we use for our TV, but it cost less than 1/5 of the price, It's got decent bass response, a little less treble, but it's not boomy. If you're expectations are realistic, you'll probably like this - it's a 16 watt bar, not 200 watts, so it won't fill your house with music and don't expect highest quality music. It does exactly what I got it for and does it well. For me, that's a big win.

I fall asleep to audiobooks, and have tried a lot of speakers and headphones with mixed results. My husband bought me these AcousticSheep SleepPhones recently, and what a difference they make! They're very comfortable - okay, the mediums are a little large for me, but I've found a way to position them so they work perfectly. The speakers are thin and pliable, so they're comfortable even if you roll over and lie on them, and the sound is pleasant - not too boomy or too shrill, and you can move the headband so you can listen in both ears or only one, if you prefer.

The one catch is that the wires leading out of the headphones are pretty thin, and judging my previous experience using many headsets and speakers in bed, they're going to break inside at some point. Then I'll either have to order more or perhaps do a little creative wire work and attach new, stronger wires. I'd be perfectly happy to replace these once a year as they've improved my quality of sleep (I'm used to waking when I roll onto a hard plastic speaker or earphone).

BTW, the headband itself is sooo soft and comfy - none of the headbands I've used on my hair over the years are this cozy.

Like it said on the package, these truly are pajamas for your ears ;-)

***Update Feb 9, 2014***

It's been just short of a year since I write the above review. Since then, I ordered a second smaller pair of SleepPhones, the band of which wasn't as soft and furry, but it was good for wearing when doing housework.
